cues: Let it stay as long as it wants.
Staying with it, without checking, is the whole of the work.
The jolt, the fast heart, maybe that thump.
Now listen for the second voice.
You don't have to answer it.
Turn towards the feeling, like a curious scientist.
Let it be as strong as it wants.
Let your breath be soft and slow on its own.
Breathe around the feeling, not against it.
Imagine floating on warm, still water.
The water holds you, and the feeling moves through.
Waves rise, peak, and fall, in their own time.
Your only job is to let the seconds go by.
Whatever the wave is doing now (higher, lower, or the same), it is allowed to be here.
Now step back into your day.
Pick up the next ordinary thing, and let the feeling come along if it wants.
You met the wave without fighting it.

This is calm-time practice: training for your nervous system, like a gentle gym.
Sit comfortably, eyes open or closed.
Breathe in gently through your nose, and out a little longer.
If your mind wanders, that's fine.
Notice where it went, and come back to the next breath.
Let your breathing find its own rhythm again.
Notice whatever your body feels now, without needing it to be anything.
A little every day is how this skill grows.
The pull to check is here.
You don't have to push it away, and you don't have to obey it.
Name it in a word, each time it changes.
If the thought says, "just one quick check", you can answer:
what did the last check really give me, ten minutes later?
Every urge you notice and ride makes the next one weaker.
This is your worry time: early in the evening, never in bed.
Open the worry river and look at today's paper boats.
For each one, ask: is there one small next step I can take?
If it's a health "what if", there is no step.
When the time is up, close it.
Tomorrow's worries can wait for tomorrow's worry time.
The worries are parked for tonight.
Lie back, and let the bed take your weight.
If your heart is noticeable, let it be noticeable.
You don't need to listen to it.
If a thought comes, let it pass by, like a boat on the river.
You don't need to climb aboard.
Sleep can't be forced, and it doesn't need to be.
Thirty seconds for your weather check: how was the night, and what's the weather inside today?
Let's just do today, even a tiny bit.
Before you start: what does the anxiety predict, and how sure is it?
Then do it fully: no checking, no escaping early.
Now write what actually happened, and how you coped.
The gap between the forecast and what happened is how the brain learns.
Here you bring on a feeling on purpose, for a short time, and see what really happens.
Make it as strong as you can.
Keep going about thirty seconds after the feeling starts.
No checking, no sitting down to recover, no breathing tricks.
Then rate it, let it settle by itself, and go again.
Keep your eyes open, resting on one spot.
First you'll focus on one sound at a time, then switch quickly between them, then hear them all at once.
Let them, and return to the sounds.
This is a gym for your attention.
Nothing needs to be done about it.
If you're calm, stay and rest.
If you're upset and wide awake for a while, get up, go to another room, and keep the light dim.
Do something quiet you chose in the daytime.
If your body feels strange as you wake, let it be there, like weather.
When you feel sleepy, go back to bed.
Tomorrow, get up at your usual time, whatever the night was like.
